catalog_quote: 3.6.1 Stress on Non-Verbs. Primary stress occurs in almost all the words in the Gizrra language. The stress falls on the first syllable. Words that consist of more than three syllables have the primary stress (ˈ) on the first syllable and an additional secondary stress (ˈˈ) on the third syllable. [ˈɑ.kul] 'shell sp.' [ˈpɛ.lɑm] 'eel' ... [ˈku.gu.pi] 'hole' [ˈdi.di.bur] 'garden' ... [ˈgjɛ.gɨp.ˈˈsu.ru] 'throat' [ˈmɪŋ.gɨ.ˈˈpɑ.nɑn] 'close by' Some exceptions are: [gə.ˈdɑm] 'friend' [bɨ.ˈsɑi] 'quick' [mɨ.ˈrɑg] 'sheet, page' [mu.ˈrɑus] 'close' [bək.ˈtɑn] 'talk' [ɑ.ˈprɑ.pəɾ] 'maybe' [dɑ.ˈrum.bi.ˈˈrə] 'jew's harp' In some words the primary stress moves to the second syllable when a suffix is added: [ˈnə.ɾɛs] 'sand' [nə.ˈɾɛs.də] 'on the sand' ... 3.6.2 Stress on Verbs. In verbs the stress falls on different syllables, depending on the grammatical suffix. The present participle has the stress on the first syllable. When the grammatical suffix is /-ɑ/ '1/2NPst', /-ɛ/ '3NPst', /-i/ 'dl.NPst', /-əp/ '1/3pl.Pst', /-(ə)rɛ/ '1/3pl.NPst', /-ɑnɛ/ '2pl.NPst', /-ɑrɛ/ '2pl.Pst', /-nənəmɑ/ '1/2sg.NPst', or /-ɑm/ 'nsg.IMP', the stress falls on the first (prefix) syllable. When the suffix is /-əm/ 'PURP', /-(ə)rə/ '1/2Pst', /-(ə)ri/ 'dl.Pst', or /-ər/ '3Pst', the stress falls on the second (root) syllable. ... [ˈɑmkɑl] hit-PRES.PART 'hit' [ˈɛ-mkəl-ɑ] 3DO-hit-1/2NPst 'I hit him (non-past)' ... [ɑmˈkɑl-əm] hit-PURP 'to hit' [ɛ-mˈkɑl-ərə] 3DO-hit-1/2Pst 'I hit him (past)'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (20 pp., pp. 191-210 of Data Papers on PNG Languages 47; volume attribution independently confirmed in the DP series list in Lock 2011 DP57 back matter held under : '47 2005 Phonological Descriptions of PNG Languages, edited by Steve Parker (.. Gizrra by Nico and Elly van Bodegraven..)'). The text drops IPA, so I rendered pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 198-199) as images. Sec. 3.6.1 'Stress on Non-Verbs', p. 198, reads exactly: 'Primary stress occurs in almost all the words in the Gizrra language. The stress falls on the first syllable. Words that consist of more than three syllables have the primary stress on the first syllable and an additional secondary stress on the third syllable.' follow…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of non-verbs; words longer than three syllables carry primary stress on syllable 1 and secondary stress on syllable 3. A handful of lexical exceptions have second-syllable stress, and some nouns shift stress to the second syllable under suffixation. In inflected verbs stress falls on either the prefix syllable or the root syllable, determined by which TAM/person suffix is present. No contrastive tone (sec. 3.4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of more than three syllables, secondary stress on the third syllable (e.g. [ˈgjɛ.gɨp.ˌsu.ru] 'throat', [ˈmɪŋ.gɨ.ˌpɑ.nɑn] 'close by').
new_statements.exceptions: Listed lexical exceptions with 2nd-syllable stress ('friend', 'quick', 'sheet', 'close', 'talk', 'maybe', 'jew's harp'); stress shift to 2nd syllable in some nouns when a suffix (e.g. locative -də) is added; verbs: stress on prefix syllable with one set of suffixes (e.g. 1/2NPst, 3NPst, nsg.IMP) and on root syllable with another (PURP, 1/2Pst, dl.Pst, 3Pst); present participle stressed on first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms from a c. 2,000-item wordlist (Kulalae village data mainly); authors distinguish word stress from sentence-level intonation (sec. 3.4). The earlier OPD (2004, p. 3) agrees: stress 'most often on the first syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Data primarily from Kulalae village (east bank of the Pahoturi), with some from Waidorro and Kolmet; authors report only small dialect differences. Language = Gizrra [tof], glottocode gizr1240 (OPD spells it 'Gizra'). No sub-dialect glottocodes involved.
